summary: Describes using keyed MD5 with the IP Authentication Header to authenticate packets. It was standards-track but is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A secret-ingredient fingerprint recipe used to show an Internet packet is genuine.

subtitle: Using MD5 to authenticate IP packets without encryption

tldr.problem: Internet Protocol needs a way to authenticate that packets come from the claimed sender and have not been modified in transit, without necessarily encrypting them.
tldr.mechanism: The IP Authentication Header (AH) carries an HMAC (keyed message digest) calculated from a shared secret key. The digest is computed over a padded key, the invariant fields of the IP datagram with variant fields zeroed, and the key again, using the MD5 algorithm to produce a 128-bit authentication value.
tldr.outcome: This mechanism, standardized in August 1995, provided packet-level authentication for the nascent IPsec architecture. However, MD5 collisions were soon discovered to be computationally feasible, and the standard was eventually marked Historic in favor of stronger algorithms like SHA.

today: RFC 1828 is marked Historic as of August 1995. It specified the use of keyed MD5 with the IP Authentication Header as part of the original IPsec architecture. However, weaknesses in MD5 (collisions in the compression function, and potential attacks on the algorithm itself) led to its replacement by stronger hash functions. Modern IPsec implementations use HMAC-SHA-256 and other stronger algorithms. New implementations must not use this mechanism for security-sensitive applications.

sections.title: IP Authentication with Keyed MD5
sections.content:
The IP Authentication Header (AH), defined in RFC 1826, provides integrity and authentication for IP datagrams. This document specifies how to use the keyed MD5 algorithm within the AH mechanism. All implementations that claim conformance with the AH specification MUST implement this keyed MD5 mechanism.

The approach uses keyed MD5 (also called HMAC-MD5), where a shared secret key is combined with the message data before computing an MD5 digest. This differs from simple MD5, where no key is used. The shared key SHOULD be cryptographically strong (not guessable) and can be of any length, though implementations must support at least 128 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Two computers share a secret password. They mix it with their message and run it through a fingerprinting algorithm. The fingerprint proves only someone with the password could have created it.

sections.title: How Keyed MD5 Calculation Works
sections.content:
The keyed MD5 digest is computed in a specific order. First, the variable-length shared secret key is padded to the next 512-bit boundary using the standard MD5 padding technique. Then the padded key is concatenated with the IP datagram (with all variant fields set to zero), concatenated with the original unpadded key again.

The form of the authenticated message is: key, keyfill, datagram, key, MD5fill. This sandwich construction—key before and after the message—provides keying that matches the construction used for message authentication in SNMPv2.

The MD5 algorithm then calculates the 128-bit digest of this entire assembled message, and that digest is inserted into the Authentication Data field of the AH header. The 128-bit output of MD5 is naturally 64-bit aligned, so typically no further padding is required in the AH field.
sections.plainLanguage: Take the secret password, pad it, add the message, add the password again, and run the whole thing through the MD5 fingerprint maker. The resulting fingerprint is the proof that someone with the secret password created this message.

sections.title: Performance and Security Issues
sections.content:
Performance: MD5 software implementations run at adequate speeds for typical LAN and WAN links of the 1990s, but are reportedly too slow for newer, faster link technologies. The document seeks suggestions for alternative algorithms with significantly faster throughput that are still not patent-encumbered and retain cryptographic strength.

Security issues: At the time of writing (August 1995), it was already known that collisions could be produced in the MD5 compression function, though no practical attack on keyed MD5 had been demonstrated. A theoretical attack suggested it might be possible to build a machine for $10 Million that could find two chosen texts with a common MD5 hash value in about 24 days.

The document cautions that while there is no substantial weakness for most IP security applications at that time, the pace of cryptanalysis and computing advances means current technology is catching up to the 128-bit hash length. Applications requiring extremely high security should consider moving in the future to algorithms with longer hash lengths.
sections.plainLanguage: MD5 is reasonably fast, but there are theoretical attacks against it that get better every year. It was a good solution in 1995 but not meant to be permanent.

sections.title: Historic Status and Deprecation
sections.content:
RFC 1828 was published as a Standards Track specification in August 1995 with the expectation that it would be the normative specification for AH keyed MD5. However, cryptographic advances and attacks on MD5 eventually rendered it obsolete. The RFC is now marked Historic.

Modern IPsec implementations use stronger algorithms such as HMAC-SHA-256 and other hash functions with greater cryptographic strength and longer digest sizes. The transition from MD5-based authentication to stronger algorithms is complete in deployed systems, and new implementations should not use this mechanism.

This RFC serves as a historical record of early IPsec authentication mechanism design and demonstrates the importance of choosing cryptographic algorithms with conservative security margins when designing for long-term deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is marked Historic, which means it was a real standard once but is not anymore. MD5 turned out not to be strong enough, so people use better fingerprint algorithms now.
